title: Written Calculations
description: Using column methods for addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, and understanding the order of operations (BIDMAS).

notes.heading: Column Addition and Subtraction
notes.body: When adding or subtracting large numbers, write them in columns with digits lined up by place value (ones under ones, tens under tens). Always start from the rightmost column. In addition, if a column sums to 10 or more, carry the extra digit to the next column. Example: 478 + 296 = 774 (8+6=14 carry 1; 7+9+1=17 carry 1; 4+2+1=7). In subtraction, if a digit is too small, borrow from the next column.

notes.heading: Short and Long Multiplication
notes.body: Short multiplication: multiply a number by a single digit, carrying extras. Example: 347 × 6 = 2082. Long multiplication: for multiplying by two or more digits, write each partial product on a new row shifted left, then add them. Example: 34 × 27 = 34×7 + 34×20 = 238 + 680 = 918.

notes.heading: Short and Long Division
notes.body: Short division (bus stop): divide by a single digit working left to right, carrying remainders. Example: 756 ÷ 3 = 252. Long division: for dividing by multi-digit numbers, use divide-multiply-subtract-bring down. Example: 672 ÷ 16 = 42.

notes.heading: Order of Operations — BIDMAS
notes.body: BIDMAS: Brackets first, Indices (powers), Division & Multiplication (left to right), Addition & Subtraction (left to right). Example: 3 + 4 × 5 = 3 + 20 = 23, NOT 7 × 5 = 35. With brackets: (3 + 4) × 5 = 35.

notes.heading: ⚠️ Common BIDMAS misconception
notes.body: Never add before you multiply just because the addition appears first. Always do division and multiplication before addition and subtraction, working from left to right. Example: 8 + 2 × 5 = 8 + 10 = 18, NOT 10 × 5 = 50.

notes.heading: ✅ Estimation checks
notes.body: Before you calculate, round the numbers to quickly estimate the answer. Example: 497 × 6 is about 500 × 6 = 3000. After working it out (2982), check it is close to your estimate. If it is not, you may have made a mistake.

flashcards.definition: The value of a digit based on its position — ones, tens, hundreds, etc.
When a column adds to 10+, write the ones digit and carry the tens to the next column.
When a digit is too small, borrow 1 from the next left column (reduce it by 1) and add 10 to current digit.
Multiply by each digit of bottom number separately, write results shifted left, then add.
Division by a single digit: work left to right, carrying remainders.
Order of operations: Brackets, Indices, Division & Multiplication (L→R), Addition & Subtraction (L→R).
Amount left after division when numbers don't divide exactly.
The result of multiplying two or more numbers.
The result of subtracting one number from another.
A rough calculation used to check if an answer is sensible.

questions.explanation: Add column by column: 6+8=14 (write 4 carry 1), 3+4+1=8, 2+7=9, 5+3=8. Answer: 8 984.

questions.stem: A school orders 15 boxes of pencils. Each box has 24 pencils. How many pencils total?
A coach travels 215 km on Monday and 178 km on Tuesday. How far does it travel in total?
questions.explanation: Add 215 + 178 column by column: 5+8=13 (write 3 carry 1), 1+7+1=9, 2+1=3. The coach travels 393 km.

questions.stem: Is it always, sometimes, or never true that multiplying two whole numbers gives a larger answer than adding them? For example, 2 × 2 = 4 and 2 + 2 = 4.
questions.explanation: It depends on the numbers. For 1 and 5, 1×5=5 but 1+5=6 (adding gives more). For 3 and 3, both give 6. For 4 and 5, multiplying gives more. So it is sometimes true.

questions.stem: A shop sells notebooks in packs of 6 for £8 and single notebooks for £1.50 each. A class needs 50 notebooks. What is the cheapest way to buy them?
questions.explanation: 8 packs give 48 notebooks for 8×£8=£64. Need 2 more singles: 2×£1.50=£3. Total £67. 7 packs = 42 notebooks (£56) + 8 singles (£12) = £68. 9 packs = 54 notebooks (£72). So 8 packs and 2 singles is cheapest.
